title: Francis de Sales (1567–1622)
hookLine: a gentle bishop who taught that everyone can be devout, in any job

cards: Doors stay shut. A young priest has been sent into a region of the Alps where the people had become Protestant, and nobody wants to hear him preach. Some days he gets no audience at all.
So he writes short leaflets explaining the Catholic faith plainly, and tradition says he slipped them under doors. The Church now calls him a patron of writers and journalists.
He would become a bishop known less for winning arguments than for his gentleness. Today, Francis de Sales.

teach.h: BISHOP OF GENEVA, LIVING IN ANNECY.
teach.b: First, a bishop without his city. Francis was named bishop of Geneva, but Geneva was a Calvinist city, so he lived and worked in nearby Annecy.
He preached, heard confessions and answered piles of letters from people trying to live their faith. Second, a book for everyone.

teach.h: DEVOTION FOR EVERY KIND OF LIFE.
teach.b: Out of those letters came his Introduction to the Devout Life, addressed to a reader he calls Philothea, a name meaning one who loves God. His point: devotion isn't only for monks and nuns.

It must fit the life you actually have. A soldier, a shopkeeper, a servant, a married woman, a prince: each is devout differently. He compares it to bees, which take honey from flowers without spoiling them.

teach.h: DON'T RAGE AT YOUR OWN FAULTS.
teach.b: Real devotion, he says, makes your work and your home better, not worse. Third, gentleness with yourself. He warns against getting angry at yourself for your faults.
When you fall, he says, don't rage. Pick yourself up gently, with sorrow but without fury, and begin again. Fourth, gentleness as strength.
Tradition says Francis was hot-tempered by nature, and his calm was hard won.

teach.h: A TEMPER IN A STEADY HAND.
teach.b: That's why his gentleness meant something: not weakness, but a temper held in a steady hand.
Catholics hear his kind of gentleness in Jesus's words in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart."

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Francis de Sales, and his Introduction to the Devout Life is still read by laypeople; Salesian religious orders carry his name, and Catholic writers and journalists keep him as their patron.

games.q: you're a young priest in the Alps. the people won't come to hear you preach, and doors stay shut. what do you do?
o: write short leaflets and slip them under the doors.
games.why: tradition says he wrote leaflets and slipped them under doors, which is why he's a patron of writers and journalists.

practice: Bring to mind one fault from this week and notice how you usually talk to yourself about it: a shout, a sigh, a long list.

Now try it Francis's way: name it plainly, be sorry, then speak to yourself as you'd speak to a friend who made the same mistake, and begin again. If you pray, hand the fault to God; if not, simply set it down.

wordCard.voice: Philothea. The name Francis de Sales gave the reader of his book, one who loves God, written to show that devotion can fit any kind of life.

carryVoice: Your line: gentleness is strength. Every fall is a place to begin again. See you tomorrow.
